name: Stable Dependencies and Package Design
intent: Arrange packages so that dependencies form no cycles and point toward the packages that change least, so a change stays local, packages can be built and released one at a time, and the shared base is small and calm instead of a grab bag.
scenario: The same product, with seven to thirteen packages, is described as data in three ways: a tangled design with a utils package that everything uses and a cycle between orders, billing and customers; a layered design with no cycles and small stable bases (money, text); and an over-split design with an api package and an impl package for everything. For each, the model computes instability, cycles, what a change to each package rebuilds, and builds per quarter from assumed change counts.
problem: A package is a unit that is built, tested, versioned and released together. When package A depends on B, a change to B can break A, so every dependency is a promise that B will not change much. If the dependencies form a cycle, none of the packages in it can be built, tested or released alone, and a team that owns one of them cannot move without the others. If a package that changes often, such as a utils package full of unrelated helpers, is depended on by everything, every change to it rebuilds and retests the whole system. Package design is the work of choosing the direction of each arrow so that this does not happen.

howItWorks.title: Measure how stable a package is
howItWorks.text: Count Ca, the packages that depend on it, and Ce, the packages it depends on. Robert Martin's instability is I = Ce / (Ca + Ce): 0 for a package that others use and that uses nothing (hard to change, so stable), 100 in percent for one that uses others and is used by nobody (easy to change, so unstable). In the layered design money has I = 0 and web has I = 100. A stable package is not good or bad; it is one that is costly to change, and so should change rarely.

howItWorks.title: Depend toward stability
howItWorks.text: The Stable Dependencies Principle says an arrow should point from a less stable package to a more stable one. A violation is an arrow to something less stable than yourself: you have promised to follow a package that moves more often than you do. The tangled design has 2 violations, one of them utils, which looks stable (I = 16, because 5 packages use it) but depends on customers (I = 40). The layered design has 0, and the over-split design has 0.

howItWorks.title: Keep the graph acyclic
howItWorks.text: The Acyclic Dependencies Principle says no package can reach itself by following dependencies. In the tangled design orders uses billing, billing uses customers and customers uses orders, and utils uses customers too: 4 packages that must be built, tested and released together, so any change to one rebuilds all of them. Cycles are broken by moving the shared piece into a new package that both depend on, or by inverting one arrow: the lower package defines an interface and the higher one implements it.

howItWorks.title: Make the shared base small and calm
howItWorks.text: A change to utils, changed 12 times a quarter in this model, rebuilds and retests 7 of 7 packages. The layered design splits it into money (1 change a quarter) and text (2), so the helper that everything uses almost never changes, and the helper that changes often is used by only a few. Package builds per quarter fall from 241 to 117. A package that everyone depends on has to be stable: either it is small and finished, or it is not a good thing to depend on.

howItWorks.title: Do not split further than the change pattern
howItWorks.text: Giving every module an api package and an impl package makes a change to an implementation cheap (2 of 13 packages rebuild), but 13 packages are 13 things to version and keep in step, and a feature that crosses layers edits 5 packages instead of 3. The builds per quarter hardly move: 113 against 117 in the layered design. Split where things change at different speeds or are owned by different teams, not on principle.

pros: A change rebuilds and retests only its dependents, so a small change has a small blast radius
Packages with no cycles can be built, tested, versioned and released one at a time, in order
Stable base packages make new code cheap to write: it can rely on them not moving
Instability and cycle counts can be computed from the import graph by a tool, so they can be checked in the build
cons: More packages mean more build files, versions and release steps to keep in order
Breaking a cycle means introducing an interface or a new package, which is work with no new feature
Instability is a ratio over the current graph: it says nothing about how often a package really changes, so it needs real change history alongside
The principles come from languages and build systems where a package is a release unit; in a single compiled module the same ideas apply to namespaces and folders more loosely
whenToUse: Multi-package, multi-module or multi-team code bases, where a build or a release unit is a real cost
When a small change rebuilds or retests most of the system, or when two packages can only be released together
Deciding where a new shared helper, a shared type or an interface should live
As a check in CI: fail the build when a new dependency creates a cycle
whenNotToUse: Splitting a small code base into many packages to follow the principle: a single module with sensible folders needs no release units
Treating a high instability number as a defect: the leaves of the graph, such as the web layer, should be unstable
Extracting an interface package for every class, when only a few things really change at different speeds
Forcing a shared utils package to be 'stable' by freezing it: split it by reason to change instead
pitfalls: A utils or common package that everything depends on and that keeps growing: it is stable by position and unstable by change history, so each edit rebuilds the whole system
A cycle that creeps in through one convenience import: orders needs one function from customers, customers needs one type from orders, and the two can no longer be built apart
Depending on a package that changes more often than you do, so each of its releases becomes your breaking change
Putting a shared type in the higher-level package so that the lower one has to import it, which closes a cycle; put it in a package both can depend on
Over-splitting into an api and an impl package for everything: 13 packages to maintain and 5 edited by a feature that cuts across layers, for almost the same build count
Judging stability by position alone: check how often a package actually changes in version control, because a central but busy package is the real cost
Fixing a cycle by merging the packages without asking whether the dependency direction was wrong: you remove the symptom and keep the coupling

roles.label: Stable base
roles.description: A small package that others use and that uses almost nothing: money, text.

roles.label: Domain package
roles.description: Orders, billing and customers: where the business rules live.

roles.label: Utils package
roles.description: Unrelated helpers that everyone imports and that changes often.

roles.label: Leaf package
roles.description: The web layer: unstable on purpose, nothing depends on it.

roles.label: Build and release
roles.description: Rebuilds and retests whatever depends on a changed package.

quiz.question: A utils package is used by 5 of 7 packages and is changed 12 times a quarter. Which problem does this create?
options: Every change to utils rebuilds and retests most of the system.
It is too unstable to be used by other packages at all.
It must be merged into the web package to be released.
Its instability rises to 100 as more packages use it.
quiz.explanation: Many dependents plus frequent change is the expensive combination: each edit forces all of them to rebuild. Instability actually falls as dependents are added. The fix is to split it by reason to change.

quiz.question: Orders uses billing, billing uses customers, and customers uses orders. What is the cost of this cycle?
options: None, as long as each package compiles by itself.
The three packages become slower at run time because of the cycle.
The cycle forces the packages to use an interface in each direction.
None of the three can be built, tested or released without the others.
quiz.explanation: Packages in a cycle form one unit: a change to any of them can break the others, so they have to move together. It is a build and release cost, not a run-time one. Moving the shared piece into a new package breaks it.

quiz.question: A team gives every module an api package and an impl package. What does the simulation show about the result?
options: Far fewer builds per quarter, since implementations are hidden behind interfaces.
A cycle between each api package and its impl package, which have to be released together.
More packages and more edits per cross-layer feature, with builds per quarter about the same.
Higher instability for every api package, since each of them has an implementation behind it.
quiz.explanation: Here the over-split design has 13 packages, a cross-layer feature editing 5 packages instead of 3, and 113 builds per quarter against 117. Implementation changes get cheaper, but the whole is not much better.
